title: Optimizing Agent Planning for Security and Autonomy
pdf_path: papers/Optimizing Agent Planning for Security and Autonomy.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker injects instructions through external data sources. The user, planner LLM, and tool implementations are trusted; jailbreaks, direct prompt injection, and tool poisoning are out of scope. Security relies on IFC labels and policies plus human approval.
core_contributions: Defines HITL load and TCR@k as autonomy metrics for IFC-protected agents
PRUDENTIA: policy- and label-aware planning on top of FIDES
Strategic variable expansion and a plan tool that predicts policy failures before acting
Endorsement: one human endorsement replaces many per-call approvals
AgentDojo o3-mini TCR@0 59.1% versus FIDES 50.1% and Basic-IFC 35.5%
WASP: zero ASR and zero HITL across four models
limitations: IFC guarantees security, not general safety or model-error-free behavior
HITL approval/endorsement UI can itself be manipulated; no user study
No declassification, so contextual downgrading is unsupported
Security assumes correct labels, correct policies, trusted runtime, and careful human review
GPT-4o is a counterexample: PRUDENTIA HITL 23.8 versus FIDES 7.8, and TCR@0 is lower
HITL load counts only successful tasks, creating selection bias
No adaptive attacks or ASR measurement on AgentDojo; WASP tasks are data-independent
Token and monetary costs can be 1.9-5.9x FIDES
theoretical_crypto_links: None; 'provable' refers to inherited IFC guarantees under correct labels/policies, not a cryptographic reduction
No cryptographic primitive, security game, theorem, or proof
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed data provenance and capability gateways are our inference; IFC variable hiding is runtime encapsulation, not encryption
evidence_refs: pp.3-5 IFC background and autonomy metrics
pp.16-20 result tables and cost/turn overhead

title: Breaking and Fixing Defenses Against Control Flow Hijacking in Multi-Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/Breaking and Fixing Defenses Against Control Flow Hijacking in Multi-Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker controls a single piece of untrusted content read by a delegated sub-agent. The content is disguised as an error and a helpful repair instruction; the orchestrator receives it from a trusted agent and re-plans into an unsafe action. The user and all agents are otherwise benign.
core_contributions: Shows control-flow hijacking attacks that evade alignment checks from multiple advanced LLMs
Argues that safety and functionality objectives structurally conflict in multi-agent systems
CONTROLVALVE: a task-specific CFG plus natural-language edge rules generated before any untrusted content is ingested
Runtime checks at each agent-to-agent transition with permit/reject/re-plan
Zero ASR on all tested IPI/CFH settings while preserving benign performance
Reduces accidental policy violations from 56% to 13%
limitations: CFG and edge rules are LLM-generated and may be wrong, too broad, or too strict
No adaptive attacker who knows the CFG/rules and searches for compliant-but-harmful payloads
Runtime judge still reads attacker-controlled traces and may be prompt-injected
CFG constrains inter-agent transitions, not tool calls inside a black-box sub-agent
No agent identity authentication; assumes message provenance and registry are trusted
Small samples, no confidence intervals, one Magentic-One configuration
No code artifact; several internal numeric inconsistencies
theoretical_crypto_links: None; control-flow integrity is a systems property, not cryptographic integrity
No security game, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed agent manifests, mTLS, and per-edge capability tokens are our inference; they authenticate origin but not contextual appropriateness
evidence_refs: pp.3-6 CFH, alignment evasion, CONTROLVALVE design
pp.7-9 main results and benign performance
pp.31-32 example CFG and edge rules

title: Monitoring Decomposition Attacks with Lightweight Sequential Monitors
pdf_path: papers/Monitoring Decomposition Attacks with Lightweight Sequential Monitors.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker decomposes a harmful goal into benign-looking subtasks across multiple turns, so no single prompt appears harmful. A monitor observes the cumulative prompt history and must halt before the harmful index. The main evaluation uses static decomposition attacks and PAIR, not a monitor-aware adaptive attacker.
core_contributions: DecomposedHarm: a benchmark of decomposed harmful tasks across agent, image, and QA settings
A lightweight sequential monitor that reads cumulative context and decides halt/continue
Shows prompt engineering alone can make GPT-4o-mini competitive with much larger monitors
GPT-4o-mini test F1 0.918, above o3-mini 0.836, GPT-4o 0.870, and GPT-5 0.887
93% defense success rate under random subtask injection
Much lower cost and latency than reasoning-model monitors
limitations: Only three task types and English
Balanced 50/50 evaluation; precision, FPR, and deployment base rates are not reported
Monitor input appears to be prompt history; tool calls/observations may not be included
PAIR is a general jailbreak, not an adaptive monitor-aware attacker
Harmful index is partly constructed/labeled and only sampled for human verification
No training/fine-tuning comparison; prompt engineering only
Single-step halt, no repair or re-planning
Internal inconsistencies: 4,634 vs 4,639, 10 vs 12 models, cost/latency wording
theoretical_crypto_links: None; monitor and decomposition attack are runtime detection and jailbreak concepts
No security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Attested monitor execution and signed audit logs are our inference; they ensure monitoring happened, not that its semantic judgment is correct
evidence_refs: pp.5-7 monitor formulation and main results
pp.8-9 injection, PAIR, and adaptive-prompt results
pp.16-30 dataset, prompt, and cost appendices

title: VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents
pdf_path: papers/VPI-Bench_Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: An opportunistic black-box attacker places visual prompts in webpages, popups, messages, or emails. The attacker does not know the user's prompt or agent architecture. The sandbox pre-configures resources needed by the malicious task, and payloads are paired with benign tasks.
core_contributions: End-to-end VPI threat model from injection to harmful outcome
VPI-Bench: 306 interactive test cases across five platforms
Evaluates two computer-use and six browser-use agents in a sandbox
Computer-use agents reach 51.3% SR; browser-use agents reach 100% SR on one cell
Five-category behavior analysis (success, partial, failed, no recognition, recognition)
System prompt and built-in defenses provide only limited improvement
limitations: Sandbox pre-configures target resources; SR is conditional on resource existence
Static, non-adaptive payloads
Payloads are paired with benign tasks, weakening the 'attacker does not know the task' premise
CUA and BUA use different case sets; framework and defense layer are confounded
No benign control or utility measurement
Judge validation only 100 traces; one tested model is also a judge
No real deployment or user study
Several internal numeric and table inconsistencies
theoretical_crypto_links: None; visual prompt injection is a semantic perception/instruction attack
No security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
OS/tool capability gating, signed provenance, and egress DLP are our inference; provenance authenticates content source, not whether content is an instruction
evidence_refs: pp.4-6 threat model and benchmark construction
pp.7-10 agent results, behavior analysis, defenses
pp.16-24 appendices with cases, judge, and compute

title: ChatInject: Abusing Chat Templates for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/ChatInject_Abusing Chat Templates for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker controls a tool response and injects a payload formatted with the target model's chat-template special tokens, forging system/user/assistant role boundaries. The attacker cannot see the user instruction or agent prompt. A multi-turn variant embeds a persuasive dialogue inside one tool response.
core_contributions: ChatInject: formats malicious payloads to mimic native chat templates
Multi-turn variant that embeds generated dialogue in a single tool response
Mixture-of-Templates attack for unknown backbones
Raises InjecAgent ASR from 15.13% to 45.90% and AgentDojo from 5.18% to 32.05%
Shows cross-model template transfer and that five prompt-based defenses are largely ineffective
Provides template-similarity and attention analyses
limitations: Assumes raw special tokens survive tool-output rendering; no real serving-framework escaping test
Template similarity is computed on proxy models, not the attacked models
No real template stripper implemented; perturbation bypass is inferred
Only five static prompt-based defenses; no instruction-hierarchy training or adaptive detector
Main table covers six open models; three closed models are only transfer targets
ASR counts only full task completion; partial harm is missed
No cost/latency or real deployment study
Several internal table and numbering inconsistencies
theoretical_crypto_links: None; chat template is a token format, not a cryptographic structure
Role tags are unauthenticated labels; similarity is hidden-state cosine, not indistinguishability
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Tool-output escaping, signed source provenance, and action-level capabilities are our inference; signing role labels cannot change the model's template/role perception
evidence_refs: pp.16-24 appendices with prompts, similarity, and attention
